segments.say: Morning comes, grey and soft, with the sound of rain on the window. Ruth wakes slowly. Biscuit is already at the side of the bed, tail going. She lies still for a moment and listens to the inside of her head. And there's nothing there. No chorus, no folk tune, just the rain and the dog. The earworm that followed her all evening has gone, just as the diary studies said most do by the next day.

Let's look back over Ruth's evening, because it has given us a complete tour of the science of earworms. It began with a few seconds of a chorus in a supermarket queue. It followed her onto the bus, into the kitchen, through dinner and the washing up, across the sofa and a choir folder, and finally into bed, where it played her to sleep.

Here's how it started, in the terms of the research. Recent exposure, in the shop, the most common trigger of all. A catchy melody, quick and rising and falling, with a small surprise inside it. Repetition, heard several times that week. And a quiet, idle mind, on the bus and at the sink, with room for the music to play.

And here's what kept it going. A word on the news, which brought it back through association. The silence of the kitchen, which gave the imagined music the stage to itself. The washing up, which let her mind wander. And listening to the song again before bed, which refreshed the memory just in time for the pillow.

And what calmed it down? A good book that absorbed her attention at the right level. A piece of gum that kept her inner voice busy for a while. And, at the end, simply letting it play without a struggle, until sleep came. Not one of these was a magic cure. Together, they were enough.

Rain on a window on a soft grey morning. The earworm is gone, and Ruth will probably never think about that particular chorus again, unless she hears it in the supermarket next week. That's the ordinary life cycle of an earworm: it arrives, it plays, it fades, and it leaves no trace except a small memory of a strange evening.

show.cap: Rain on a window on a grey morning

segments.say: Let's gather the big findings. In the large Finnish survey, more than nine in ten people had an earworm at least once a week. In diaries, a typical episode lasted around twenty-seven minutes. Only about a third were described as unpleasant. And most were gone by the following day. Earworms are common, short and usually harmless.

show.title: What the research tells us
items: Over 90% get one at least weekly
Typical episode: about half an hour
Most are gone by the next day

segments.say: We've also seen what makes a song stick. In Jakubowski's study of about three thousand people, sticky tunes tended to be faster, with a common rising and falling shape and a few unusual intervals. Hearing a song more times makes it more likely to loop, as the 2023 chorus experiment showed. And earworms find room when our minds wander or when a task is too hard to hold our attention.

And we've glimpsed what's happening inside. The brain's hearing areas can stay active in silence, filling in familiar music from memory. Imagined songs play at close to their real tempo. The inner voice seems to be involved, which may be why chewing gum can help. And during sleep, the brain may even replay recently heard music.

show.sub: Memory, hearing and the inner voice

segments.say: Here's a gentle guide, built from tonight's research. First, notice the trigger, because simply understanding where a tune came from can make it feel less strange. Second, don't fight it head on, because suppression often makes it worse. Third, find something that absorbs you at the right level. Fourth, if you like, try chewing gum or a slow, calm song. And fifth, give catchy music a rest before bed.

show.title: A gentle guide to earworms
items: Try gum, or a slow song
Give music a rest before bed

segments.say: But perhaps the most important point is that most earworms need nothing at all. They come and go on their own, and many of them are pleasant. If a tune is keeping you company, there's no reason to chase it away. The guide is for the stubborn ones, the occasional earworm that outstays its welcome, especially at night.

And as we said earlier, if repetitive, unwanted thoughts or sounds of any kind are causing real distress, lasting a long time or getting in the way of everyday life, it's worth speaking with a doctor. That's true of any persistent experience that worries you. But for most people, most of the time, an earworm is simply a sign of a healthy musical memory at work.

It's worth coming back, for a moment, to Mark Twain. In 1876, he joked about a jingle that could only be cured by passing it on. A century and a half later, researchers have shown that earworms really do travel through shops, radios and other people's humming, and that they draw on deep features of how memory works. Twain's joke turned out to contain a real insight.

If there's one thought to keep from tonight, perhaps it's this. Your mind holds a vast library of music, gathered over a lifetime, from lullabies and school songs to the chorus in last week's supermarket. Every so often, that library starts playing by itself. It can be annoying. But it's also a small reminder of how much your memory carries, and how alive it is.

Ruth gets up, pulls on a jumper and lets Biscuit out into the rainy garden. She fills the kettle. As it starts to hum, she half expects the chorus to return. It doesn't. Instead, she finds herself humming something new, a few notes of the folk tune from her choir folder, slow and gentle. She smiles. Thursday is only two days away.

So, in this final part of Ruth's story, the earworm has gone, as most do by the next morning. We've gathered the findings, from the prevalence surveys to the sleep laboratory, and built a gentle guide: notice the trigger, don't fight it head on, find something absorbing, try gum or a slow song, and give music a rest before bed.

And now, if you're listening at the end of your own day, it's time to wind down. In the next part, we'll let the ideas go and settle into a slow, quiet rest, with nothing to remember and nothing to work out.
